prize_parts.citation: for establishing modern political economics by analysing how constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes

statement.case_for: B016 gave economics a formal and empirical programme for how electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and political agency determine fiscal policy and development. It is a coherent body of work with about three decades of theory, cross-country and within-country empirical follow-up, and it is standard across public economics, development and political economy. It is mature, so there is no timing concern. The grouping is also the one most colleagues who rank B016 converge on (six of the eleven rank it, all with the same three names), so attribution is not a disputed point. The case rests on conceptual contribution and field-building rather than on a single estimate. That distinguishes it from candidates whose strength is mainly a method or a recent data programme.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is identification. Constitutions and electoral systems are not randomly assigned, so many of the cross-country constitutional-effects estimates are correlational or rest on contested instruments, and from my own credibility-oriented perspective this weakens the evidential side of the case. The second reservation is thematic overlap with the 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity, which could be read as redundancy. The third is that the credit split between the Persson–Tabellini and Besley–Persson strands is hard to apportion, and adjacent contributors (Acemoglu, Robinson, Dixit and the late Alesina) are outside this ballot item.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B016 third and notes that thematic proximity to the 2024 institutions prize could cut either way. He also raises contested identification in cross-country constitutional comparisons and discloses Swedish-institutional proximity.
responses.response: I accept the overlap risk but think it is overstated. The 2024 award concerned how historically determined institutions explain long-run differences in prosperity across countries. B016 concerns the mechanics inside political systems: how electoral rules, constitutional design and agency problems map into taxation, spending and public-goods provision. These are complementary questions, and the 2024 recognition shows the Committee regards the area as important rather than closed. I agree on identification. That is why I would frame the citation around the analytical framework and the programme it generated, not around any single causal estimate. I agree that the proximity issue should be disclosed and not adjudicated, as the protocol says, and I do not treat it as evidence for or against the candidates.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B016 third. He finds the three-name set natural but says Alesina, Acemoglu and Dixit have strong claims in adjacent parts of the field. He also flags contested identification and partial overlap with the 2024 prize.
responses.response: I agree that the boundary is a judgement call, but I think it can be drawn principledly. Persson and Tabellini built the unifying theoretical and empirical framework on constitutions and policy outcomes. Besley, with Persson, developed state capacity and political agency. Alesina cannot be credited posthumously. Acemoglu and Robinson's institutions work is already recognised in 2024. Dixit's contributions are earlier and sit mostly in other strands. So the three-name set is the cleanest cut of the specific contribution in B016, and widening it would blur the achievement rather than sharpen it. On identification, I would stress that the later empirical literature has moved to better designs within countries, so the programme is stronger than the early cross-country estimates suggest.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B001 first. She sees Grossman–Helpman as a clean two-person attribution with a durable explanatory framework (protection for sale) and decades of extension.
responses.response: I agree that B001 has the cleaner attribution and is fully mature, which is why I rank it second and name it as an alternative. My hesitation has two parts. Empirical support for the protection-for-sale prediction is acknowledged by several colleagues, including Andersson, to be mixed. Helpman is also tied to B020, where four members rank firm heterogeneity first, so a committee that chose B001 would implicitly be choosing which of Helpman's bodies of work to recognise. I do not think this reduces B001's merit. I do think B016's contribution is less entangled with other ballot items. The attribution advantage of B001 is real, but it is not decisive for me given the breadth of B016.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B019 first. She values the transparent, heavily scrutinised designs of the import-competition evidence and considers the core results robust to follow-up work.
responses.response: I rank B019 third and share her respect for design-based evidence on a first-order policy question; this is the kind of work I find most credible in my own field. My reservations are about attribution and the debate on the evidence. The task framework has important co-originators outside the credited set, and the choice among Dorn, Katz and others is contested. Debate over shift-share identification, exposure measurement and long-run persistence is continuing. None of this disqualifies B019, and I name it as an alternative. But I find the contribution in B016 more cleanly bounded and more settled as a body of work, even though its identification is weaker than that of B019's best designs.

uncertainties: How much weight the Committee places on conceptual and field-building contributions when the identification of the underlying causal claims is contested.
Whether the 2024 institutions prize makes a political-economics award read as redundant or as a natural complement.
Whether the Persson–Tabellini and Besley–Persson strands should be treated as one achievement, and whether three names is the right cut.
How to weigh B001 against B016: B001 has cleaner two-person attribution and broader top-three support, but Helpman's overlap with B020 and mixed empirical support complicate it.
I have not independently verified citations or priority claims; the assessment relies on the supplied committee materials and my recollection of the literature.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My profile lists no co-authorship with the B016 candidates and no co-authorship with the B001, B019 or B031 candidates. I overlapped institutionally with the IIES macro group at Stockholm University in 2010–17, but my profile does not identify any candidate affiliation with it. Colleagues have flagged possible Swedish-institutional proximity of some B016 candidates to the Committee. I note this and do not adjudicate it.
